title: Atherosclerosis: Fatty Streaks, Fibrous Caps, Foam Cells, and Response to Injury

steps.tx: The contemporary pathophysiological model of atherogenesis is the **response-to-injury hypothesis**, which views atherosclerosis as a chronic, non-resolving inflammatory response of the arterial wall to endothelial perturbation. Repeated hemodynamic shear stress, hypercholesterolemia, tobacco smoke toxins, and advanced glycation end-products cause chronic endothelial injury. Endothelial cells increase permeability, downregulate antithrombotic molecules, and upregulate leukocyte adhesion receptors (VCAM-1 and ICAM-1) that recruit circulating monocytes and T-lymphocytes into the subendothelial intima.
steps.say: Atherosclerosis is fundamentally a chronic inflammatory disease of large and medium elastic and muscular arteries initiated by endothelial injury. Hemodynamic turbulence, hypertension, cigarette smoke, and elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol damage endothelial cells. The injured endothelium expresses adhesion molecules like VCAM-1, capturing circulating blood monocytes and T-lymphocytes and ushering them into the subendothelial intimate layer.

left.title: Healthy Intact Endothelium
points: Continuous impermeable mechanical barrier
Constitutive nitric oxide and prostacyclin synthesis
Antithrombotic: expresses thrombomodulin and heparan
Minimal baseline expression of adhesion molecules

right.title: Activated Injured Endothelium
points: Increased permeability to circulating LDL particles
Upregulation of VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 adhesion molecules
Impaired nitric oxide vasodilation with local spasm
Prothrombotic state favoring platelet adhesion

steps.tx: The earliest gross morphological manifestation of atherosclerosis is the **asymptomatic fatty streak**, visible as flat, elongated yellow macules or streaks along the intimal surface of arteries. Microscopically, fatty streaks consist purely of lipid-engorged, subendothelial macrophage foam cells clustered beneath an intact endothelial monolayer, accompanied by scattered T-lymphocytes. Fatty streaks emerge in the aorta of virtually all children older than one year of age and carry zero hemodynamic significance, with some evolving into mature fibrofatty plaques while others regress.
steps.say: Fatty streaks are the earliest visible lesions of atherosclerosis, appearing as flat, yellow intimal spots or ribbons inside the aorta in virtually all children over one year of age. Under the microscope, fatty streaks contain only lipid-laden macrophage foam cells and a few T-cells trapped under an intact endothelial surface. They cause no blood flow obstruction and can either resolve completely or progress over decades into advanced atheromatous plaques.

rows: Flat, yellow intimal spots or streaks <1 cm
Intimal macrophage foam cells, few T-cells
Lipid core with overlying fibrous cap
Triggers acute myocardial infarction or stroke
Focal ballooning dilation of arterial wall
Media thinned by loss of elastic lamina

steps.tx: Slice mentally through the wall of this artery. Nearest the lumen lies a pale fatty streak, beneath it sit swollen foam cells stuffed with lipid, and deeper still is a soft necrotic centre covered by a firmer fibrous roof. That layered structure is the mature **atheromatous plaque**, whose cap thickness decides whether it quietly narrows the vessel or suddenly ruptures.
steps.say: Cut through this artery wall and you see foam cells over a soft necrotic core, roofed by a fibrous cap. That layered atheromatous plaque can narrow the vessel quietly or rupture suddenly.

steps.tx: Macrophage transformation into **lipid-laden foam cells** represents the central cellular engine of atherogenesis. Circulating low-density lipoproteins enter the intimate layer where oxygen free radicals oxidize them into oxidized LDL. Uncontrolled by normal feedback inhibition, macrophage scavenger receptors (scavenger receptor A and CD36) internalize oxidized LDL particles via receptor-mediated endocytosis. The cytoplasmic vesicles become engorged with cholesteryl esters, creating lipid vacuoles that impart a bubbly, foamy appearance while stimulating secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
steps.say: Foam cells form when macrophages swallow vast amounts of oxidized cholesterol. Low-density lipoprotein trapped in the intima becomes oxidized by reactive oxygen species. While normal LDL receptors shut off when the cell is full of lipid, macrophage scavenger receptors CD36 and scavenger receptor A lack feedback downregulation. They endlessly ingest oxidized LDL, engorging the cytoplasm with lipid droplets that turn the cells into bubbly, foamy macrophages.

left.title: Macrophage Scavenger Receptors
points: Receptors: Scavenger Receptor A (SR-A) and CD36
High affinity for oxidized, chemically modified LDL
Zero feedback downregulation by intracellular lipid
Drives continuous foam cell transformation

right.title: Classical Native LDL Receptors
points: Receptors: Clathrin-coated pit LDL receptors
Binds native, unmodified low-density lipoproteins
Tightly regulated by intracellular cholesterol content
Internalization stops when intracellular sterols rise

steps.tx: A mature atheromatous plaque exhibits a well-demarcated bipartite anatomical architecture. The superficial luminal surface is shielded by a **protective fibrous cap** composed of smooth muscle cells, abundant dense collagen types I and III, elastin, and extracellular matrix. Beneath the cap lies the central necrotic lipid core, containing amorphous extracellular cholesterol crystals, necrotic foam cell debris, calcium deposits, and tissue factor. Platelet-derived growth factor secreted by macrophages stimulates medial smooth muscle cells to migrate into the intima and synthesize matrix.
steps.say: A mature atheroma has two distinct structural zones. Covering the luminal surface is a dense fibrous cap made of smooth muscle cells, collagen fibers, and proteoglycans. Beneath this protective cap lies a necrotic lipid core packed with dead foam cells, extracellular cholesterol clefts, and procoagulant tissue factor. Growth factors released by macrophages coax medial smooth muscle cells to migrate into the intima and produce the collagen cap.

rows: Dense, hyalinized collagen fibers with smooth muscle
Protects plaque from luminal shear stress rupture
Amorphous debris, foam cell ghosts, cholesterol clefts
Highly thrombogenic reservoir of tissue factor
High density of macrophages, T-cells, mast cells
Weakest site where matrix breakdown precipitates rupture
Thinned, atrophic muscular media with neo-vessels
Degraded vascular smooth muscle and elastin
Wall weakening leading to aneurysm formation

steps.tx: Clinical vulnerability of an atherosclerotic plaque to acute rupture depends on its mechanical composition rather than the degree of luminal stenosis. A **vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque** features a thin, attenuated fibrous cap measuring less than sixty-five micrometers in thickness, a large necrotic lipid core occupying more than forty percent of total plaque volume, and intense macrophage infiltration within the shoulder regions. Active macrophages secrete matrix metalloproteinases (interstitial collagenases and gelatinases) that continuously degrade the collagen skeleton, precipitating catastrophic plaque rupture.
steps.say: Plaques that rupture and cause heart attacks are often not the severely stenotic ones, but rather vulnerable plaques. A vulnerable plaque has a thin fibrous cap under sixty-five micrometers, a massive necrotic lipid core occupying over forty percent of its volume, and dense macrophage infiltration at the shoulders. Macrophages release matrix metalloproteinases that digest collagen faster than smooth muscle cells can synthesize it, leaving the cap paper-thin and prone to tearing.

left.title: Vulnerable (Unstable) Plaque
points: Thin fibrous cap (<65 um thickness)
Large, soft necrotic lipid core (>40% volume)
Dense inflammatory macrophage infiltrate at shoulders
High risk of acute rupture and occlusive thrombosis

right.title: Stable Atherosclerotic Plaque
points: Thick, dense, collagenous fibrous cap
Small, fibrotic, calcified necrotic core
Minimal inflammatory macrophage activity
Causes chronic exertional angina without acute rupture

steps.tx: Severe advanced atherosclerosis represents the leading cause of **abdominal aortic aneurysm development**. As atheromatous plaques expand, the diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from the lumen to the inner media is compromised. Furthermore, chronic transmural inflammation releases elastases and collagenases that destroy the medial elastic lamellae. Medial atrophy and fibrosis weaken wall tensile strength, causing progressive aneurysmal dilation typically located below the renal arteries and above the aortic bifurcation, predisposing patients to life-threatening rupture when diameter exceeds 5.5 centimeters.
steps.say: Atherosclerosis is the primary driver of abdominal aortic aneurysms. As thick atheromas coat the aortic intima, they block oxygen diffusion from the bloodstream into the underlying muscular media, while chronic inflammation degrades the elastic framework. The weakened aortic wall balloons outwards, usually in the infrarenal segment. The risk of fatal rupture rises sharply when the aneurysm diameter exceeds five point five centimeters.

vis.alt: Abdominal computed tomography showing infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm with mural thrombus
vis.caption: Atherosclerotic abdominal aortic aneurysm on CT, a late wall weakening complication.

steps.tx: The proximate trigger for ninety percent of acute myocardial infarctions and acute coronary syndromes is **acute plaque disruption**, manifesting as fibrous cap fissure, rupture, or superficial intimal erosion. Cap rupture exposes the intensely thrombogenic necrotic core directly to flowing luminal blood. Circulating platelets adhere to exposed subendothelial collagen and von Willebrand factor, while tissue factor activates the extrinsic coagulation cascade. Within minutes, a layered occlusive thrombus (lines of Zahn) forms, completely obliterating arterial lumen and precipitating downstream transmural myocardial infarction.
steps.say: Acute myocardial infarction occurs when an unstable atherosclerotic plaque cracks or tears open. Cap rupture exposes the necrotic lipid core and tissue factor directly to the bloodstream. Platelets immediately adhere, activate, and aggregate to form a primary hemostatic plug, while thrombin generation creates a dense fibrin network. Within minutes, an occlusive thrombus blocks coronary blood flow, starving the downstream myocardium and triggering acute ischemic necrosis.

steps.tx: The catastrophic acute clinical endpoint of abdominal aortic aneurysmal disease is **spontaneous aneurysm rupture**, which carries an overall mortality rate exceeding eighty percent. Rupture occurs most frequently through the posterolateral aortic wall into the retroperitoneal space, presenting with the classical clinical triad of excruciating tearing lower back or abdominal pain, a pulsatile tender abdominal mass, and profound circulatory shock. Immediate computed tomography angiography confirms retroperitoneal haematoma, and emergency open or endovascular repair is mandatory to prevent exsanguination.
steps.say: Rupture of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is a catastrophic surgical emergency with mortality exceeding eighty percent. Rupture typically occurs into the retroperitoneum, producing a classic clinical triad: sudden severe tearing back or flank pain, a tender pulsatile abdominal mass, and profound hemorrhagic shock. Survival depends on immediate emergency diagnosis and rapid transfer to the operating room for open vascular clamping or endovascular balloon occlusion.

vis.alt: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showing ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm with extensive retroperitoneal hematoma
vis.caption: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, the catastrophic endpoint of atherosclerotic wall weakening.

quiz.q: Which morphological characteristic defines a vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque predisposed to acute rupture?
options: Thin fibrous cap (<65 um) with large necrotic lipid core and macrophage shoulder infiltrates
Thick collagenous fibrous cap with extensive dense dystrophic calcification
Pure collection of subendothelial foam cells covered by an intact endothelial monolayer
Concentric laminated smooth muscle cell hyperplasia with luminal onion-skinning
quiz.explain: Vulnerable plaques possess a thin fibrous cap (<65 um), a large necrotic lipid core (>40% of plaque volume), and dense macrophage infiltrates secreting matrix metalloproteinases that degrade collagen.

quiz.q: What is the earliest gross morphological lesion identified in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis?
options: Fatty streak composed of subendothelial macrophage foam cells
Fibrofatty atheromatous plaque with central necrotic core
Mural thrombus with lines of Zahn
quiz.explain: Fatty streaks are flat, yellow intimal lesions composed of lipid-laden macrophage foam cells, appearing in young children and representing the earliest stage of atherogenesis.

quiz.q: What anatomical diameter threshold indicates elective surgical or endovascular repair for an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm in men?
quiz.explain: The risk of spontaneous rupture increases exponentially beyond 5.5 cm in men (5.0 cm in women), serving as the clinical threshold for elective repair.
